meta.title: Who really said "There are three sorts of people: the living, the dead, and those at sea"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Aristotle and not Plato. The joke belongs to Anacharsis, the Scythian sage, recorded by Diogenes Laërtius: asked whether the living or the dead were more numerous, he replied by asking which group you put sailors in.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are three sorts of people: the living, the dead, and those at sea'?
meta.ogDescription: It is Anacharsis, in Diogenes Laërtius — and in the original it is not a statement at all but a counter-question, which is what makes it funny.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — it is Anacharsis, and it is a question
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th century BC · Scythian sage, remembered among the wise men of Greece
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely ancient, but it belongs to Anacharsis, not Aristotle. It is preserved by Diogenes Laërtius in the Lives of the Eminent Philosophers: asked whether the living or the dead were more numerous, Anacharsis answered with a question — ‘Under which head do you class those who are at sea?’ Note what the modern version does to it. The original is a needle: a refusal to accept the terms of the question. The famous rewrite flattens it into a tidy statement of three categories, loses the joke, and hands it to a more famous Greek.
answer.confidenceText: Real, ancient, and by the wrong man.

source.excerpt: Under which head do you class those who are at sea?
trail: The genuine text is in Diogenes Laërtius, the third-century AD compiler who collected the philosophers’ sayings and comebacks. In the section on Anacharsis, he records that the sage was asked whether the dead or the living were more numerous, and replied by asking where sailors belong. The English above is C. D. Yonge’s 1853 translation the sourced text ↗.

The Aristotle credit has no document behind it. Nothing resembling the line appears in the surviving Aristotelian corpus, and the treatises are among the most thoroughly indexed bodies of text in existence — an unlocated Aristotle sentence is a strong signal that there is no Aristotle sentence.

The Plato version fails too. The line is regularly hunted for in the Critias and the Timaeus, presumably because both dialogues concern the sea and Atlantis. It is in neither. Anacharsis, meanwhile, has the saying under his own name in a standard reference work, which is about as clean as ancient attribution gets.
source.cutTag: Diogenes Laërtius I, 'Anacharsis' 5 (trans. C. D. Yonge, 1853)
source.excerptNote: Anacharsis’ actual reply, in Yonge’s Victorian English. He had been asked a binary question — living or dead, which are there more of — and instead of answering he pointed at the men on the water, who are, in the only sense that matters to their families, neither.

author.name: Aristotle
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Aristotle
author.bio: Aristotle is the default name for any ancient-sounding line that classifies things, because classifying things is genuinely what he did — he sorted animals, arguments, governments and virtues into categories for a living. A sentence that opens ‘there are three sorts of people’ therefore sounds like him before you have read the rest of it. That is precisely the trap: the modern rewrite was made to sound Aristotelian by turning Anacharsis’ question into a taxonomy, and the disguise worked.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is unusual and rather satisfying: the quotation is genuinely ancient, the real speaker is known and sourced, and the only things wrong with the popular version are the name on it and the fact that it has stopped being a joke.

items.why: Nothing like it survives in the Aristotelian treatises, which are exhaustively indexed. Yet the credit has enough momentum that it has needed correcting in the pages of academic journals the published correction ↗.
Diogenes Laërtius records it in his section on Anacharsis: asked whether the living or the dead were more numerous, he asked in return where you would put those at sea the sourced text ↗.

items.who: Not in the Critias or the Timaeus
items.why: The two dialogues most often named are the two most concerned with the sea, which is likely why people go looking there. It is in neither — nor anywhere else in Plato.
You will see the line dated to 45 BC and given to Cicero. No passage has ever been produced, and the attribution appears only in modern quotation collections.

Anacharsis asked a question that refuses the premise; the modern version answers it with a tidy list of three categories. The rewrite is what makes it quotable and also what kills the point — the whole force of the original is that he will not tell you the answer.

misattribution.truthLine: Anacharsis the Scythian, recorded in Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers I, ‘Anacharsis’ 5 — and in the original it is a counter-question, not a classification the source ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: For anyone who has waited on shore for a ship, the line is not a paradox but a description. A sailor at sea is not dead, but he is not present either — and for months at a time nobody on land can tell you which of the two he is. That is why it has been quoted for centuries by seafaring people and printed in maritime journals.

It carries better as a question than as a statement. Anacharsis was not proposing a third category of human being; he was pointing out that the question he had been asked could not be answered honestly, which is a very different and much sharper move.
detailsBody: A Scythian, from the steppe north of the Black Sea — a foreigner among Greeks, which is the whole basis of his reputation.
He was remembered for blunt outsider’s questions that exposed what the Greeks took for granted, and some ancient lists count him among the wise men of Greece.
Almost nothing survives of him directly. What we have comes through later compilers, chiefly Diogenes Laërtius.
That is also why his name loses out to Aristotle’s: a good line attached to an unfamiliar name tends to migrate to a famous one.
context.pull: He was not naming a third kind of person. He was refusing to answer the question.
